newsitem.title: USA: US House panel okays airwave auction legislation.
newsitem.headline: US House panel okays airwave auction legislation.

text.p: A House subcommittee narrowly approved legislation Tuesday that would set minimum bids at federal airwave auctions and allow regulators to postpone auctions in which bids are considered too low.

The legislation, approved 13-12 by the telecommunications subcommittee, is a part of a bill intended to implement the recent fiscal 1998 budget pact agreed to by President Clinton and approved by Congress.
The pact calls for the government to raise $26.3 billion over the next five years through spectrum auctions -- a figure that even lawmakers on the panel said is unrealistically high.
Rep Edward Markey, D-Mass., said a shortfall would be "inevitable."

The provisions for minimum bids and other steps follow a recent Federal Communications Commission auction that fell well short of the $1.8 billion Congress was counting on to help cut the deficit. Some wireless communications licenses in that auction sold for as little as $1 each.

The auction legislation also contains a provision allowing television broadcasters -- in the transition to high-definition digital TV -- to keep their existing analog licenses if five percent of the viewers in their market still use the analog technology by the year 2007.
Markey was unsuccessful in pushing legislation that would have required all sets before then to contain the technology needed to receive digital broadcasts.
Under current law the analog licenses are supposed to be auctioned for other uses and broadcasters must then return those licenses following the transition to digital broadcasts.
"There's no date certain for a return of this spectrum," Markey said.
The legislation is scheduled to be voted on by the House Commerce Committee on Wednesday. The Senate is working on separate legislation.
